intro: You already know break the ice and a piece of cake. Today you'll add sixteen idioms for work, conflict and success (cut corners, clear the air, pay off), fixed pairs like pros and cons and sooner or later, and the real C1 skill: knowing when an idiom helps and when plain words are better. Warm-up: think of a group project where one person did almost nothing. How did the team deal with it?
teachingNotes: Build on b2-phrasal-verbs-idioms: the learner knows what an idiom is (a fixed group of words you can't translate word by word) and eight idioms: break the ice, a piece of cake, under the weather, on the same page, cost an arm and a leg, hit the nail on the head, call it a day, the ball is in your court. They also know that the words are fixed and that idioms are informal. Recap that in one line; don't re-teach those idioms. This is a C1 vocabulary lesson reached straight after B2: use A0–B2 grammar only (no inversion, cleft sentences, subjunctive, impersonal passives or advanced participle clauses in examples).

Sixteen idioms in three groups, each with an Indonesian gloss. Work: cut corners (mengorbankan kualitas / keamanan demi hemat waktu atau biaya; always negative), go the extra mile (berusaha lebih dari yang diminta), pull your weight (mengerjakan bagianmu dengan adil; often negative: He isn't pulling his weight), get the ball rolling (memulai), back to the drawing board (kembali ke titik nol), a (steep) learning curve (banyak yang harus cepat dipelajari, berat di awal). Conflict: clear the air (membicarakan masalah secara terbuka supaya suasana tidak tegang), see eye to eye (sepaham; mostly negative: don't see eye to eye), be at loggerheads with sb / over sth (bersitegang; common in news), bury the hatchet (berdamai; hatchet = kapak kecil), sweep sth under the carpet (menutup-nutupi masalah; American: under the rug). Success / failure: pay off (membuahkan hasil, terbayar; pay off a loan = melunasi), hit the ground running (langsung tancap gas), a long shot (peluang kecil tapi tetap dicoba), fall through (batal; not 'jatuh'), make or break (penentu berhasil atau gagal; a make-or-break meeting with hyphens before a noun).

Indonesian bridges and where the picture differs: back to the drawing board ≈ kembali ke titik nol (same idea, different picture); pay off ≈ terbayar (same picture); hit the ground running ≈ tancap gas (car vs runner); not pulling your weight ≈ the 'numpang nama' member of a kerja kelompok (but numpang nama is only about getting credit in a group). Warn: cut corners is NOT potong kompas (a shortcut route or skipping procedure): cut corners always means quality or safety goes down. Don't translate Indonesian idioms word for word (panjang tangan is not 'long-handed'; makan hati is not 'eat the liver'); a few have true twins (air mata buaya = crocodile tears, kambing hitam = a scapegoat, besar kepala = big-headed).

Fixed form, the node's common errors: words, number and articles are fixed: *'a piece of cakes' → a piece of cake; *'break ice' → break the ice (Indonesian has no 'the', so learners drop it); *'the extra kilometre' → the extra mile. But the grammar around the idiom works normally: tense (It paid off, The deal fell through, They buried the hatchet), possessive (she isn't pulling her weight) and the object in the middle (sweep the problem / it under the carpet). Binomials (pasangan kata tetap): two words joined by and / or in a fixed order: *'Let's look at the cons and pros' → the pros and cons. Teach pros and cons, by and large (secara umum), sooner or later (cepat atau lambat), give and take, trial and error (coba-coba), ups and downs (pasang surut, suka duka), safe and sound, first and foremost, odds and ends. Indonesian has binomials too, sometimes in the same order (pro dan kontra, cepat atau lambat), sometimes not (jual beli → buying and selling; keluar masuk → in and out). There is no reliable rule for the order: learn each pair as one piece.

Appropriateness is a judgment, and much of it is style: say so honestly. Clear cases only: idioms fit chats, conversation, meetings, informal emails and speeches; plain language is better in academic writing, formal reports (ministry, board, investors) and with listeners whose English is limited (international calls), where idioms get lost. Avoid tired or outdated idioms (raining cats and dogs → It's pouring) and business clichés (think outside the box); one idiom used well beats five. Binomials are mostly neutral (pros and cons, trial and error, by and large work in meetings and most reports; odds and ends is informal; in a formal academic essay 'advantages and disadvantages' is safer), but don't test those fine lines.

Test meaning from context with clearly different distractors, form with one clear answer (missing word, tense, pair order), and register only where the context makes the choice obvious. Don't add more idioms unless the learner asks; if they do, give the meaning, an Indonesian gloss and whether it's informal. Accept British and American variants (under the carpet / under the rug, cancelled / canceled).

keyPoints.title: Idioms for work, conflict and success
keyPoints.explanation: Learn each idiom as one piece, with its meaning. Work: cut corners (lower quality to save time or money), go the extra mile, pull your weight, get the ball rolling, back to the drawing board, a steep learning curve. Conflict: clear the air, see eye to eye (mostly negative), be at loggerheads, bury the hatchet, sweep it under the carpet. Success and failure: pay off, hit the ground running, a long shot, fall through, make or break. The words and articles are fixed (a piece of cake, break the ice), but the tense and possessive change: It paid off. She isn't pulling her weight.

examples.en: The contractor cut corners, and the roof started leaking after a month.
examples.id: Kontraktornya mengorbankan kualitas, dan atapnya mulai bocor setelah sebulan.

examples.en: After two years of silence, the two brothers finally buried the hatchet at Lebaran.
examples.id: Setelah dua tahun tidak saling bicara, kakak-beradik itu akhirnya berdamai saat Lebaran.

examples.en: Our social media campaign paid off: sales doubled in March.
examples.id: Kampanye media sosial kami membuahkan hasil: penjualan naik dua kali lipat di bulan Maret.

id.title: Idiom seputar kerja, konflik dan kesuksesan
id.explanation: Pelajari setiap idiom sebagai satu kesatuan, lengkap dengan artinya. Kerja: cut corners (mengorbankan kualitas demi hemat waktu atau biaya), go the extra mile (berusaha lebih), pull your weight (mengerjakan bagianmu), get the ball rolling (memulai), back to the drawing board (kembali ke titik nol), a steep learning curve (banyak yang harus cepat dipelajari). Konflik: clear the air (meluruskan masalah), see eye to eye (sepaham; biasanya dalam kalimat negatif), be at loggerheads (bersitegang), bury the hatchet (berdamai), sweep it under the carpet (menutup-nutupi). Sukses dan gagal: pay off (membuahkan hasil), hit the ground running (langsung tancap gas), a long shot (peluang kecil), fall through (batal), make or break (penentu berhasil atau gagal). Kata dan artikelnya tetap (a piece of cake, break the ice), tapi tense dan kata kepemilikannya berubah: It paid off. She isn't pulling her weight.

keyPoints.title: Binomials: fixed pairs in a fixed order
keyPoints.explanation: A binomial is two words joined by and / or in a fixed order: pros and cons (not cons and pros), by and large (in general), sooner or later, give and take, trial and error, ups and downs, safe and sound, first and foremost, odds and ends. Indonesian has them too, sometimes in the same order (pro dan kontra, cepat atau lambat), sometimes not (jual beli → buying and selling). There's no reliable rule: learn each pair as one piece.

examples.en: By and large, the new trains in Jakarta run on time.
examples.id: Secara umum, kereta-kereta baru di Jakarta berangkat tepat waktu.

examples.en: Sooner or later, every startup has to make a profit.
examples.id: Cepat atau lambat, setiap startup harus menghasilkan untung.

examples.en: I learned to cook rendang by trial and error.
examples.id: Saya belajar memasak rendang dengan coba-coba.

id.title: Binomial: pasangan kata dengan urutan tetap
id.explanation: Binomial adalah dua kata yang digabung dengan and / or dalam urutan yang tetap: pros and cons (bukan cons and pros), by and large (secara umum), sooner or later (cepat atau lambat), give and take (saling memberi dan menerima), trial and error (coba-coba), ups and downs (pasang surut), safe and sound (selamat), first and foremost (yang paling utama), odds and ends (barang atau urusan kecil-kecil). Bahasa Indonesia juga punya, kadang urutannya sama (pro dan kontra, cepat atau lambat), kadang tidak (jual beli → buying and selling). Tidak ada aturan pasti: hafalkan setiap pasangan sebagai satu kesatuan.

keyPoints.title: When an idiom fits, and when plain language is better
keyPoints.explanation: Idioms fit chats, conversation, meetings, informal emails and speeches. Use plain language in academic writing, formal reports, and with listeners whose English is limited (international calls), where an idiom can get lost. Avoid tired idioms (raining cats and dogs → It's pouring) and don't use too many. Don't translate Indonesian idioms word for word: panjang tangan isn't 'long-handed'.

examples.en: Team chat: "Great news, guys: all those late nights paid off!"
examples.id: Chat tim: "Kabar baik, teman-teman: semua lembur itu terbayar!"

examples.en: Report to the ministry: "The pilot programme achieved its targets."
examples.id: Laporan untuk kementerian: "Program percontohan itu mencapai targetnya."

id.title: Kapan idiom cocok, dan kapan bahasa biasa lebih baik
id.explanation: Idiom cocok untuk chat, obrolan, rapat, email santai dan pidato. Pakai bahasa yang sederhana dan langsung di tulisan akademik, laporan formal, dan dengan pendengar yang bahasa Inggrisnya terbatas (rapat online internasional), karena idiom bisa tidak dipahami. Hindari idiom yang sudah usang (raining cats and dogs → It's pouring) dan jangan terlalu banyak. Jangan menerjemahkan idiom Indonesia kata per kata: panjang tangan bukan 'long-handed'.

guidedPractice.prompt: Complete with one word: The test users found the new app very confusing. OK, team: back to the ___ board.
guidedPractice.hint: kembali ke titik nol: think of the table where a designer draws a plan.

guidedPractice.prompt: Complete with one word: The hotel staff went the extra ___: they found Pak Hasan's laptop and sent it to Surabaya for free.
guidedPractice.hint: berusaha lebih dari yang diminta. The idiom keeps the old English unit, not kilometre.

guidedPractice.prompt: Put 'fall through' in the past simple: Our plan to open a café in Yogyakarta ___ because the rent was too high.
Put the pair in the right order (foremost / and / first): ___, the safety of our staff matters more than profit.
guidedPractice.hint: yang paling utama: the short, everyday word comes first.

guidedPractice.prompt: Dr. Wulan is writing a journal article. Is this a good sentence for it? 'Finding a cheaper method was a long shot, but in the end it paid off.' Write yes or no.
guidedPractice.hint: Think about the kind of text: academic writing prefers plain words to idioms.

independentPractice.prompt: Complete with one word: To get the ball ___, Bu Ani asked everyone to share one idea for the new product.
independentPractice.hint: memulai: the ball starts to move.

independentPractice.prompt: Write the English fixed pair for 'pasang surut' (good times and bad times).
independentPractice.hint: Both words are plural, and the good one comes first.

independentPractice.prompt: On a call with partners from Vietnam, Sari wants plain words. Replace 'bury the hatchet' with two plain words: Both teams need to ___.
independentPractice.hint: berdamai: say it with simple everyday words.

assessment.prompt: Complete the idiom with one word: In our group assignment, Budi never does his share of the work, and the rest of us always have to finish his part for him. He doesn't pull his ___.
assessment.rubric: Correct: weight (pull your weight = mengerjakan bagianmu dengan adil). 'weights' = 50 (the idiom is fixed: singular). 'part' / 'share' / 'job' = 30 (the right idea, but not the idiom). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: Complete the idiom with one word: Rina and her manager don't ___ eye to eye on remote work: she wants two days a week at home, but he wants everyone in the office every day.
assessment.rubric: Correct: see (see eye to eye = sepaham; here negative: they disagree). 'saw' / 'seen' / 'seeing' = 40 (the right idiom, but after don't you need the base form). 'look' / 'meet' = 10 (the words of an idiom are fixed). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: Complete with 'pay off' in the right form: Rina studied for the IELTS every evening for six months, and last week it finally ___: she got a 7.5.
assessment.rubric: Correct: paid off (past simple, because of 'last week'; the idiom's words stay, only the verb changes). 'payed off' = 70 (right idea, but the past of pay is paid). 'has paid off' = 60 (present perfect doesn't go with 'last week'). 'pays off' / 'pay off' = 40 (wrong tense). 'paid' without off = 30 (that's about money, not success).

assessment.prompt: Complete the fixed pair with one word: There were a few problems with the new payroll system in the first week, but by and ___, the staff are happy with it.
assessment.rubric: Correct: large (by and large = secara umum, pada umumnya; a fixed pair). 'larger' = 40 (the words of the pair are fixed). 'big' / 'far' = 10 (not the fixed pair). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: Correct the mistake and write only the corrected fixed pair: 'Before we choose a supplier, let's list the cons and pros of each one.'
acceptableAnswers: lets list the pros and cons of each one
let's list the pros and cons of each one
let us list the pros and cons of each one
before we choose a supplier lets list the pros and cons of each one
before we choose a supplier let's list the pros and cons of each one
before we choose a supplier let us list the pros and cons of each one
assessment.rubric: Correct: pros and cons (a fixed pair: the order never changes; pro dan kontra). The whole corrected sentence is also full marks. 'advantages and disadvantages' = 70 (correct English, but it replaces the pair instead of fixing it). 'pro and con' / 'pros and con' = 50 (right order, but both words are plural). 'cons and pros' unchanged = 0.

assessment.prompt: Rina is writing a formal report for a ministry. Her draft says: 'Unfortunately, the agreement with the Malaysian distributor fell through.' Replace 'fell through' with plain, formal words (one to three words).
acceptableAnswers: unfortunately the agreement with the malaysian distributor was cancelled
unfortunately the agreement with the malaysian distributor failed
unfortunately the agreement with the malaysian distributor did not go ahead
assessment.rubric: Correct: plain, formal words with the meaning 'didn't happen in the end' (batal): was cancelled / canceled, failed, collapsed, did not go ahead, did not proceed, was not completed / signed. 'was called off' / 'did not happen' = 80 (right meaning and plain, but less formal or vague). 'fell apart' = 50 (another informal idiom). 'was terminated' = 60 (it means an agreement that started was ended early). 'fell' alone or 'was delayed' = 0 (wrong meaning).

assessment.prompt: Pak Hasan is on a video call with a new partner from Korea whose English is basic, so he wants to avoid idioms. Replace 'a long shot' with plain words: 'Getting the import permit by Friday is a long shot.' → Getting the import permit by Friday is ___.
assessment.rubric: Correct: unlikely (or very / highly unlikely, not likely, improbable, doubtful): a long shot = peluangnya kecil, but still possible. 'almost impossible' = 70 (plain, but a bit too strong). 'difficult' / 'hard' / 'a challenge' = 60 (plain, but it's about difficulty, not the small chance). 'impossible' = 40 (too strong: there's still a chance). 'possible' / 'likely' = 0 (the doubt is lost or reversed). Another idiom = 0 (the task is plain words).

material.title: Idioms for work: cut corners, go the extra mile …

id.title: Idiom seputar kerja: cut corners, go the extra mile …

blocks.text:
**Quick recap** from B2: an **idiom** is a fixed group of words whose meaning you can't guess from each word (*under the weather* = a bit ill). You know eight: *break the ice, a piece of cake, under the weather, on the same page, cost an arm and a leg, hit the nail on the head, call it a day, the ball is in your court*.

Today you'll add sixteen, in three groups. First, six you'll hear in almost every office:
- **cut corners** = do something too cheaply or too quickly, so the **quality or safety** goes down (mengorbankan kualitas atau keamanan). Always negative.
- **go the extra mile** = do more than you have to (berusaha lebih dari yang diminta).
- **pull your weight** = do your fair share of the work (mengerjakan bagianmu dengan adil). Often negative: *He isn't pulling his weight.*
- **get the ball rolling** = start something, take the first step so things begin to move (memulai).
- **back to the drawing board** = the plan failed, so we start again from the beginning (kembali ke titik nol).
- **a learning curve** = the time it takes to learn something new. **A steep learning curve** = a lot to learn quickly, hard at the start (banyak yang harus cepat dipelajari).

id.text:
**Ulasan singkat** dari B2: **idiom** adalah kelompok kata tetap yang artinya tidak bisa ditebak dari tiap katanya (*under the weather* = agak tidak enak badan). Kamu sudah tahu delapan: *break the ice, a piece of cake, under the weather, on the same page, cost an arm and a leg, hit the nail on the head, call it a day, the ball is in your court*.

Hari ini kamu menambah enam belas, dalam tiga kelompok. Pertama, enam idiom yang akan kamu dengar di hampir setiap kantor:
- **cut corners** = mengerjakan sesuatu terlalu murah atau terlalu cepat, sehingga **kualitas atau keamanannya** turun (mengorbankan kualitas). Selalu negatif.
- **go the extra mile** = berusaha lebih dari yang diminta.
- **pull your weight** = mengerjakan bagianmu dengan adil. Sering dalam kalimat negatif: *He isn't pulling his weight.* (Dia tidak mengerjakan bagiannya.)
- **get the ball rolling** = memulai sesuatu, mengambil langkah pertama supaya semuanya mulai berjalan.
- **back to the drawing board** = rencananya gagal, jadi kita mulai lagi dari awal (kembali ke titik nol).
- **a learning curve** = waktu yang dibutuhkan untuk mempelajari hal baru. **A steep learning curve** = banyak yang harus cepat dipelajari, berat di awal.

rows.en: The contractor cut corners, and the roof started leaking after a month.
rows.id: Kontraktornya mengorbankan kualitas, dan atapnya mulai bocor setelah sebulan.

rows.en: The hotel staff went the extra mile and decorated our room for my mother's birthday.
rows.id: Staf hotel berusaha lebih dari yang diminta dan menghias kamar kami untuk ulang tahun ibu saya.

rows.en: Everyone in the team pulled their weight, so we finished early.
rows.id: Semua orang di tim mengerjakan bagiannya, jadi kami selesai lebih cepat.

rows.en: Let me get the ball rolling: here are three ideas for the anniversary event.
rows.id: Saya mulai dulu ya: ini tiga ide untuk acara ulang tahun perusahaan.

rows.en: The investors rejected our business plan, so we went back to the drawing board.
rows.id: Para investor menolak rencana bisnis kami, jadi kami mulai lagi dari nol.

rows.en: There's a steep learning curve with the new accounting software.
rows.id: Software akuntansi yang baru butuh banyak waktu untuk dipelajari, terutama di awal.

blocks.text:
**Indonesian bridges, with care.** Some of these have an Indonesian partner:
- *back to the drawing board* ≈ **kembali ke titik nol**: the same idea, a different picture (a designer's table instead of zero).
- someone who isn't *pulling their weight* is like the **numpang nama** member of a *kerja kelompok*. But *numpang nama* is only about putting your name on group work; *pull your weight* works for any shared job, at work or at home.
- **Trap:** *cut corners* is **not** *potong kompas*. *Potong kompas* is about a shortcut (a quicker route, skipping a procedure). *Cut corners* always means the **quality or safety** goes down to save time or money.

And the words stay English even in Indonesia: it's always *the extra **mile***, never 'the extra kilometre'.

id.text:
**Jembatan ke bahasa Indonesia, tapi hati-hati.** Beberapa idiom ini punya pasangan dalam bahasa Indonesia:
- *back to the drawing board* ≈ **kembali ke titik nol**: idenya sama, gambarannya beda (meja gambar desainer, bukan angka nol).
- orang yang tidak *pulling their weight* mirip anggota **numpang nama** di kerja kelompok. Tapi *numpang nama* hanya soal menaruh nama di tugas kelompok; *pull your weight* bisa dipakai untuk pekerjaan bersama apa saja, di kantor atau di rumah.
- **Jebakan:** *cut corners* **bukan** *potong kompas*. *Potong kompas* soal jalan pintas (rute lebih cepat, melompati prosedur). *Cut corners* selalu berarti **kualitas atau keamanannya** turun demi hemat waktu atau biaya.

Dan kata-katanya tetap bahasa Inggris walaupun di Indonesia: selalu *the extra **mile***, tidak pernah 'the extra kilometre'.

blocks.prompt: Rina's new job uses software she has never seen before. She tells a friend: 'There's a steep learning curve.' What does she mean?
options: The software is very easy to learn.
She has a lot to learn quickly, and it's hard at first.
Her salary will go up quickly.
blocks.explain: A steep learning curve = a lot to learn in a short time, hard at the start. It's about learning, not money, and 'steep' tells you it isn't easy.

id.prompt: Pekerjaan baru Rina memakai software yang belum pernah ia lihat. Ia bilang ke temannya: 'There's a steep learning curve.' Apa maksudnya?
id.explain: A steep learning curve = banyak yang harus dipelajari dalam waktu singkat, berat di awal. Ini soal belajar, bukan gaji, dan 'steep' (curam) menunjukkan bahwa itu tidak mudah.
options: Software-nya sangat mudah dipelajari.
Dia perlu mempelajari banyak hal dengan cepat, dan awalnya sulit.
Gajinya akan cepat naik.

material.title: Conflict and success: clear the air, pay off …

id.title: Konflik dan kesuksesan: clear the air, pay off …

blocks.text:
**Conflict** (when people disagree):
- **clear the air** = talk openly about a problem so the tension goes away (membicarakan masalah secara terbuka supaya suasana tidak tegang lagi).
- **see eye to eye (on sth)** = agree. Mostly used in the negative: *We don't see eye to eye on this* = kita beda pendapat.
- **be at loggerheads (with sb / over sth)** = be in a strong, long disagreement (bersitegang). Common in the news: *The two ministries are at loggerheads over the budget.*
- **bury the hatchet** = stop fighting and make peace (berdamai, melupakan permusuhan). A *hatchet* is a small axe (kapak kecil): you put the weapon in the ground.
- **sweep sth under the carpet** = hide a problem instead of dealing with it (menutup-nutupi masalah). American English says *under the rug*.

id.text:
**Konflik** (saat orang tidak sependapat):
- **clear the air** = membicarakan masalah secara terbuka supaya suasana tidak tegang lagi.
- **see eye to eye (on sth)** = sepaham, setuju. Biasanya dipakai dalam kalimat negatif: *We don't see eye to eye on this* = kita beda pendapat soal ini.
- **be at loggerheads (with sb / over sth)** = berselisih keras dan lama (bersitegang). Sering muncul di berita: *The two ministries are at loggerheads over the budget.*
- **bury the hatchet** = berhenti bertengkar dan berdamai. *Hatchet* adalah kapak kecil: senjatanya dikubur.
- **sweep sth under the carpet** = menyembunyikan masalah, bukan menyelesaikannya (menutup-nutupi). Bahasa Inggris Amerika memakai *under the rug*.

rows.en: Pak Hasan and his business partner rarely see eye to eye on prices.
rows.id: Pak Hasan dan mitra bisnisnya jarang sepaham soal harga.

rows.en: The union and the management are at loggerheads over the new shift system.
rows.id: Serikat pekerja dan manajemen bersitegang soal sistem shift yang baru.

rows.en: After two years of silence, the two brothers finally buried the hatchet at Lebaran.
rows.id: Setelah dua tahun tidak saling bicara, kakak-beradik itu akhirnya berdamai saat Lebaran.

rows.en: If there's a problem with the data, tell the client. Don't sweep it under the carpet.
rows.id: Kalau ada masalah dengan datanya, beri tahu klien. Jangan ditutup-tutupi.

blocks.text:
**Success and failure**:
- **pay off** = bring a good result after a lot of effort (membuahkan hasil, terbayar). Careful: *pay off a loan* = melunasi pinjaman.
- **hit the ground running** = start a new job or project and work well from the first day (langsung tancap gas).
- **a long shot** = something unlikely to succeed, but worth trying (peluangnya kecil). Think of a shot from very far away: it rarely hits.
- **fall through** = a plan or deal doesn't happen in the end (batal, gagal terwujud). Nothing falls: it isn't *jatuh*.
- **make or break** = decides whether something succeeds or fails completely (penentu berhasil atau gagal). Before a noun, use hyphens: *a make-or-break meeting*.

id.text:
**Sukses dan gagal**:
- **pay off** = membuahkan hasil setelah banyak usaha (terbayar). Hati-hati: *pay off a loan* = melunasi pinjaman.
- **hit the ground running** = memulai pekerjaan atau proyek baru dan langsung bekerja dengan baik sejak hari pertama (langsung tancap gas).
- **a long shot** = sesuatu yang peluang berhasilnya kecil, tapi tetap layak dicoba. Bayangkan tembakan dari jarak sangat jauh: jarang kena.
- **fall through** = rencana atau kesepakatan akhirnya tidak terjadi (batal, gagal terwujud). Tidak ada yang jatuh: artinya bukan *jatuh*.
- **make or break** = menentukan apakah sesuatu berhasil atau gagal total (penentu). Sebelum kata benda, pakai tanda hubung: *a make-or-break meeting*.

rows.en: Our social media campaign paid off: sales doubled in March.
rows.id: Kampanye media sosial kami membuahkan hasil: penjualan naik dua kali lipat di bulan Maret.
rows.note: pay → paid: only the tense changes

id.note: pay → paid: hanya tense-nya yang berubah

rows.en: Our new sales manager hit the ground running and signed two clients in her first week.
rows.id: Manajer penjualan kami yang baru langsung tancap gas dan mendapat dua klien di minggu pertamanya.

rows.en: Winning the government tender is a long shot, but let's try.
rows.id: Peluang kita memenangkan tender pemerintah itu kecil, tapi ayo kita coba.

rows.en: Our team trip to Lombok fell through when the budget was cut.
rows.id: Rencana jalan-jalan tim ke Lombok batal waktu anggarannya dipotong.

rows.en: This product launch is make or break for our startup.
rows.id: Peluncuran produk ini menjadi penentu hidup-matinya startup kami.

blocks.text: **Indonesian bridges:** *pay off* ≈ **terbayar** (*kerja kerasnya terbayar*): the same picture, so it's easy to remember. *hit the ground running* ≈ **langsung tancap gas**: Indonesian uses a car, English uses a runner, but the idea is the same. *at loggerheads* ≈ **bersitegang**. But read the context for the others: *fall through* is not *jatuh*, and *sweep it under the carpet* has nothing to do with cleaning.

id.text: **Jembatan ke bahasa Indonesia:** *pay off* ≈ **terbayar** (*kerja kerasnya terbayar*): gambarannya sama, jadi mudah diingat. *hit the ground running* ≈ **langsung tancap gas**: bahasa Indonesia memakai mobil, bahasa Inggris memakai pelari, tapi idenya sama. *at loggerheads* ≈ **bersitegang**. Untuk yang lain, baca konteksnya: *fall through* bukan *jatuh*, dan *sweep it under the carpet* tidak ada hubungannya dengan bersih-bersih.

blocks.prompt: Read: 'The two departments have been at loggerheads for months.' What's the situation?
options: They have worked together very well.
They have been waiting for a decision.
They have been in a strong disagreement.
blocks.explain: be at loggerheads = be in a strong, long disagreement (bersitegang). It's the opposite of working well together, and it isn't about waiting.

id.prompt: Baca: 'The two departments have been at loggerheads for months.' Bagaimana situasinya?
id.explain: be at loggerheads = berselisih keras dan lama (bersitegang). Ini kebalikan dari bekerja sama dengan baik, dan tidak ada hubungannya dengan menunggu.
options: Mereka bekerja sama dengan sangat baik.
Mereka sedang menunggu keputusan.
Mereka terus berselisih keras.

material.title: The words are fixed, the grammar isn't

blocks.text:
An idiom is **fixed**: don't change its words, make its noun plural, or drop or change *a / the*.
- **a piece of cake** ✓, not *a piece of cakes* ✗ (even if the test had ten parts)
- **break the ice** ✓, not *break ice* ✗: the *the* belongs to the idiom
- **go the extra mile** ✓, not *the extra kilometre* ✗; **It's a long shot** ✓, not *It's long shot* ✗

But the **grammar around it** works normally:
- the verb changes **tense**: *It **paid** off.* *The deal **fell** through.* *They've **buried** the hatchet.*
- the **possessive** (kata kepemilikan: my, his, her, their) changes with the person: *I pull **my** weight, she pulls **her** weight.*
- the **object** (the thing the verb acts on) can go in the middle: *sweep **the problem** under the carpet, sweep **it** under the carpet.*

id.text:
Idiom itu **tetap**: jangan ubah katanya, jangan jadikan kata bendanya jamak, dan jangan buang atau ganti *a / the*.
- **a piece of cake** ✓, bukan *a piece of cakes* ✗ (walaupun tesnya punya sepuluh bagian)
- **break the ice** ✓, bukan *break ice* ✗: kata *the* adalah bagian dari idiomnya
- **go the extra mile** ✓, bukan *the extra kilometre* ✗; **It's a long shot** ✓, bukan *It's long shot* ✗

Tapi **tata bahasa di sekitarnya** berjalan seperti biasa:
- kata kerjanya berubah **tense**: *It **paid** off.* *The deal **fell** through.* *They've **buried** the hatchet.*
- **kata kepemilikan** (possessive: my, his, her, their) berubah sesuai orangnya: *I pull **my** weight, she pulls **her** weight.*
- **objek** (hal yang dikenai kata kerja) bisa masuk di tengah: *sweep **the problem** under the carpet, sweep **it** under the carpet.*

rows.en: The quiz at the start of the workshop really broke the ice.
rows.id: Kuis di awal workshop benar-benar mencairkan suasana.

rows.en: Our plans for a second branch fell through last year.
rows.id: Rencana kami membuka cabang kedua batal tahun lalu.

rows.en: Dimas isn't pulling his weight on this project.
rows.id: Dimas tidak mengerjakan bagiannya di proyek ini.

rows.en: Rina and her old boss have buried the hatchet.
rows.id: Rina dan mantan atasannya sudah berdamai.

rows.en: The manager tried to sweep the complaint under the carpet.
rows.id: Manajer itu mencoba menutup-nutupi keluhan tersebut.
rows.note: the object goes in the middle

blocks.text: **The Indonesian trap: the missing *the*.** Indonesian has no word like *the*, so it's easy to drop it: *break ice*, *pull weight*, *clear air*. In an idiom, every small word is part of the piece. And don't 'fix' an idiom with grammar rules you know: *a piece of cake* stays singular, *ups and downs* stays plural.

id.text: **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: *the* yang hilang.** Bahasa Indonesia tidak punya kata seperti *the*, jadi mudah sekali membuangnya: *break ice*, *pull weight*, *clear air*. Dalam idiom, setiap kata kecil adalah bagian dari satu kesatuan. Dan jangan 'membetulkan' idiom dengan aturan tata bahasa yang kamu tahu: *a piece of cake* tetap tunggal, *ups and downs* tetap jamak.

options: Thanks, the quiz was a piece of cakes!
The new manager isn't pulling her weight.
Let's play a short game to break ice.
blocks.explain: pull your weight changes its possessive with the person (her weight), which is normal grammar. The other two change the fixed words: it's a piece of cake (singular) and break the ice (with the).

id.explain: pull your weight mengubah kata kepemilikannya sesuai orangnya (her weight), dan itu tata bahasa biasa. Dua kalimat lain mengubah kata yang tetap: yang benar a piece of cake (tunggal) dan break the ice (dengan the).

material.title: Fixed pairs: pros and cons, sooner or later

id.title: Pasangan kata tetap: pros and cons, sooner or later

blocks.text:
A **binomial** (pasangan kata tetap) is two words joined by *and* or *or* in a **fixed order**. Swap them and a native speaker will still understand you, but it sounds wrong: **pros and cons** ✓, *cons and pros* ✗.
- **pros and cons** = advantages and disadvantages (pro dan kontra, kelebihan dan kekurangan)
- **by and large** = in general, mostly (secara umum, pada umumnya). Don't try to translate *by* or *large*: learn it as one piece.
- **sooner or later** = at some time in the future, it will happen (cepat atau lambat)
- **give and take** = both sides give something up (saling memberi dan menerima, saling mengalah)
- **trial and error** = trying different ways until one works (coba-coba)
- **ups and downs** = good times and bad times (pasang surut, suka duka)
- **safe and sound** = safe, with no harm (selamat, tidak kurang suatu apa)
- **first and foremost** = most importantly, before anything else (yang pertama dan paling utama); good in speeches
- **odds and ends** = small things or small jobs of different kinds (barang atau urusan kecil-kecil); nothing to do with *odds* (peluang)

Most binomials are neutral: *pros and cons*, *trial and error* and *by and large* work in meetings and most reports. *odds and ends* is informal.

id.text:
**Binomial** (pasangan kata tetap) adalah dua kata yang digabung dengan *and* atau *or* dalam **urutan yang tetap**. Kalau ditukar, penutur asli tetap mengerti, tapi kedengarannya salah: **pros and cons** ✓, *cons and pros* ✗.
- **pros and cons** = kelebihan dan kekurangan (pro dan kontra)
- **by and large** = secara umum, pada umumnya. Jangan coba menerjemahkan *by* atau *large*: hafalkan sebagai satu kesatuan.
- **sooner or later** = cepat atau lambat (pasti terjadi suatu saat)
- **give and take** = saling memberi dan menerima, saling mengalah
- **trial and error** = coba-coba sampai ada cara yang berhasil
- **ups and downs** = masa baik dan masa sulit (pasang surut, suka duka)
- **safe and sound** = selamat, tidak kurang suatu apa
- **first and foremost** = yang pertama dan paling utama; cocok untuk pidato
- **odds and ends** = barang atau urusan kecil-kecil yang macam-macam; tidak ada hubungannya dengan *odds* (peluang)

Kebanyakan binomial netral: *pros and cons*, *trial and error* dan *by and large* bisa dipakai di rapat dan sebagian besar laporan. *odds and ends* santai (informal).

rows.en: We discussed the pros and cons of opening a branch in Surabaya.
rows.id: Kami membahas pro dan kontra membuka cabang di Surabaya.

rows.en: By and large, the new trains in Jakarta run on time.
rows.id: Secara umum, kereta-kereta baru di Jakarta berangkat tepat waktu.

rows.en: Sooner or later, every startup has to make a profit.
rows.id: Cepat atau lambat, setiap startup harus menghasilkan untung.

rows.en: Working in a small team means a lot of give and take.
rows.id: Bekerja di tim kecil berarti banyak saling mengalah.

rows.en: I learned to cook rendang by trial and error.
rows.id: Saya belajar memasak rendang dengan coba-coba.

rows.en: The family business has had its ups and downs.
rows.id: Usaha keluarga itu sudah mengalami pasang surut.

rows.en: Bu Ani's flight landed late, but she got home safe and sound.
rows.id: Pesawat Bu Ani mendarat terlambat, tapi ia sampai di rumah dengan selamat.

rows.en: The big jobs are done; I just have some odds and ends to finish.
rows.id: Pekerjaan besarnya sudah selesai; tinggal urusan kecil-kecil yang harus saya bereskan.

blocks.text: **Indonesian has binomials too**, and sometimes the order is the same as English: *pro dan kontra* → **pros and cons**, *cepat atau lambat* → **sooner or later**. But don't trust the Indonesian order: *jual beli* → **buying and selling** (not *selling and buying*), *keluar masuk* → **in and out** (*people going in and out*). There's no reliable rule for the order, so learn each pair as one piece, the way you learn an idiom.

id.text: **Bahasa Indonesia juga punya binomial**, dan kadang urutannya sama dengan bahasa Inggris: *pro dan kontra* → **pros and cons**, *cepat atau lambat* → **sooner or later**. Tapi jangan percaya urutan bahasa Indonesia: *jual beli* → **buying and selling** (bukan *selling and buying*), *keluar masuk* → **in and out** (*people going in and out*). Tidak ada aturan pasti soal urutannya, jadi hafalkan setiap pasangan sebagai satu kesatuan, seperti kamu menghafal idiom.

blocks.prompt: Complete: Moving to a new city always has its ___.
options: downs and ups
ups and downs
up and down
blocks.explain: The pair is fixed: ups and downs (pasang surut), with the good one first and both words plural. 'downs and ups' swaps the order; 'up and down' isn't the pair (it means naik turun, a movement).

id.prompt: Lengkapi: Moving to a new city always has its ___.
id.explain: Pasangannya tetap: ups and downs (pasang surut), yang baik di depan dan keduanya jamak. 'downs and ups' menukar urutannya; 'up and down' bukan pasangan ini (artinya naik turun, sebuah gerakan).

blocks.text:
At C1 the question isn't only *Is this idiom correct?* but *Does it fit here?* Often there's no single right answer, it's a matter of style, but some cases are clear.

**Idioms fit well** in chats and conversation with colleagues, meetings, informal emails, and speeches or presentations (one good idiom keeps people listening).

**Plain language** (simple, direct words) **is better** in:
- **academic writing** (theses, journal articles) and **formal reports** for a ministry, a board or investors: *The project was successful*, not *The project paid off*.
- **international calls and emails** where people's English is limited (partners from Japan, Korea or Brazil, or anyone still learning): idioms are cultural, and machine translation often turns them into nonsense. *She did well from her first day* is clearer than *She hit the ground running*.

**Avoid tired idioms.** *It's raining cats and dogs* is in every textbook, but most native speakers today just say **It's pouring**. Business clichés (ungkapan klise: used so often they sound empty), like *think outside the box*, can annoy readers. One idiom used well beats five tired ones.

id.text:
Di level C1, pertanyaannya bukan hanya *Apakah idiom ini benar?* tapi juga *Apakah cocok di sini?* Sering tidak ada satu jawaban yang pasti, ini soal gaya, tapi ada kasus yang jelas.

**Idiom cocok** di chat dan obrolan dengan rekan kerja, rapat, email santai, serta pidato atau presentasi (satu idiom yang pas membuat orang tetap mendengarkan).

**Bahasa yang sederhana dan langsung lebih baik** di:
- **tulisan akademik** (skripsi, tesis, artikel jurnal) dan **laporan formal** untuk kementerian, direksi atau investor: *The project was successful*, bukan *The project paid off*.
- **rapat online dan email internasional** dengan orang yang bahasa Inggrisnya terbatas (mitra dari Jepang, Korea atau Brasil, atau siapa pun yang masih belajar): idiom itu terikat budaya, dan mesin penerjemah sering mengubahnya jadi kalimat aneh. *She did well from her first day* lebih jelas daripada *She hit the ground running*.

**Hindari idiom yang sudah usang.** *It's raining cats and dogs* ada di setiap buku pelajaran, tapi kebanyakan penutur asli sekarang cukup bilang **It's pouring**. Klise bisnis (ungkapan yang terlalu sering dipakai sampai terdengar kosong), seperti *think outside the box*, bisa membuat pembaca jengkel. Satu idiom yang dipakai dengan tepat lebih baik daripada lima idiom usang.

rows.en: Team chat: "Great news, guys: all those late nights paid off!"
rows.id: Chat tim: "Kabar baik, teman-teman: semua lembur itu terbayar!"

rows.en: Report to the ministry: "The pilot programme achieved its targets."
rows.id: Laporan untuk kementerian: "Program percontohan itu mencapai targetnya."

rows.en: Speech: "This year was make or break for us, and we made it."
rows.id: Pidato: "Tahun ini penentu bagi kami, dan kami berhasil."
rows.note: a lively idiom in a speech

rows.en: It's pouring outside.
rows.id: Di luar hujan deras sekali.
rows.note: more natural than 'raining cats and dogs'

id.note: lebih alami daripada 'raining cats and dogs'

blocks.text: **Don't translate Indonesian idioms word for word.** *panjang tangan* is not 'long-handed' (say *he steals*), and *makan hati* is not 'eat the liver' (say *it really hurts me* or *it upsets me*). A few do have English twins: *air mata buaya* = **crocodile tears**, *kambing hitam* = **a scapegoat**, *besar kepala* = **big-headed**. If you aren't sure an English idiom exists, say it plainly: plain words are always safe.

id.text: **Jangan menerjemahkan idiom Indonesia kata per kata.** *panjang tangan* bukan 'long-handed' (katakan *he steals*), dan *makan hati* bukan 'eat the liver' (katakan *it really hurts me* atau *it upsets me*). Ada beberapa yang punya kembaran dalam bahasa Inggris: *air mata buaya* = **crocodile tears**, *kambing hitam* = **a scapegoat**, *besar kepala* = **big-headed**. Kalau kamu tidak yakin idiomnya ada dalam bahasa Inggris, katakan dengan kata-kata biasa: itu selalu aman.

blocks.prompt: Dr. Wulan is writing the conclusion of a journal article. Which sentence fits best?
options: Our new teaching method paid off big time.
By and large, the new method was a piece of cake for students.
The new teaching method improved students' test scores.
blocks.explain: A journal article needs plain, precise language: 'improved students' test scores' says exactly what happened. 'paid off big time' and 'a piece of cake' are informal idioms that belong in conversation, not in academic writing.

id.prompt: Dr. Wulan sedang menulis kesimpulan artikel jurnal. Kalimat mana yang paling cocok?
id.explain: Artikel jurnal butuh bahasa yang sederhana dan tepat: 'improved students' test scores' menyebut dengan jelas apa yang terjadi. 'paid off big time' dan 'a piece of cake' adalah idiom santai untuk obrolan, bukan untuk tulisan akademik.

suggestedQuestions: Can I use idioms in a job interview?
Why is it 'pros and cons' and not 'cons and pros'?
Which idioms are OK in an email to my manager?

resources.title: Improve Your ENGLISH FLUENCY with BINOMIALS
resources.note: Rebecca explains what binomials are and teaches about twenty of them, including first and foremost and pros and cons, with tips for IELTS and TOEFL. All in English; the engVid page has a 10-question quiz with pairs like sooner or later, ups and downs and safe and sound. Some pairs in the video aren't in this lesson.

id.note: Rebecca menjelaskan apa itu binomial dan mengajarkan sekitar dua puluh pasangan, termasuk first and foremost dan pros and cons, plus tips untuk IELTS dan TOEFL. Seluruhnya dalam bahasa Inggris; halaman engVid-nya punya kuis 10 soal dengan pasangan seperti sooner or later, ups and downs dan safe and sound. Beberapa pasangan di video tidak ada di pelajaran ini.

id.intro: Kamu sudah tahu break the ice dan a piece of cake. Hari ini kamu menambah enam belas idiom seputar kerja, konflik dan kesuksesan (cut corners, clear the air, pay off), pasangan kata tetap seperti pros and cons dan sooner or later, dan keterampilan C1 yang sebenarnya: tahu kapan idiom membantu dan kapan kata-kata biasa lebih baik. Pemanasan: ingat satu tugas kelompok di mana satu orang hampir tidak mengerjakan apa-apa. Bagaimana timmu menghadapinya?
suggestedQuestions: Bolehkah saya memakai idiom saat wawancara kerja?
Kenapa 'pros and cons', bukan 'cons and pros'?
Apakah 'raining cats and dogs' itu salah?
Idiom mana yang boleh dipakai di email ke atasan?

assessment.idm-1: Lengkapi idiomnya dengan satu kata: In our group assignment, Budi never does his share of the work, and the rest of us always have to finish his part for him. He doesn't pull his ___.
assessment.idm-2: Lengkapi idiomnya dengan satu kata: Rina and her manager don't ___ eye to eye on remote work: she wants two days a week at home, but he wants everyone in the office every day.
assessment.idm-3: Lengkapi dengan 'pay off' dalam bentuk yang tepat: Rina studied for the IELTS every evening for six months, and last week it finally ___: she got a 7.5.
assessment.idm-4: Lengkapi pasangan kata tetapnya dengan satu kata: There were a few problems with the new payroll system in the first week, but by and ___, the staff are happy with it.
assessment.idm-5: Perbaiki kesalahannya dan tulis hanya pasangan kata tetap yang sudah benar: 'Before we choose a supplier, let's list the cons and pros of each one.'
assessment.idm-6: Rina sedang menulis laporan formal untuk sebuah kementerian. Drafnya berbunyi: 'Unfortunately, the agreement with the Malaysian distributor fell through.' Ganti 'fell through' dengan kata-kata biasa yang formal dalam bahasa Inggris (satu sampai tiga kata).
assessment.idm-7: Pak Hasan sedang rapat video dengan mitra baru dari Korea yang bahasa Inggrisnya masih dasar, jadi ia ingin menghindari idiom. Ganti 'a long shot' dengan kata-kata biasa dalam bahasa Inggris: 'Getting the import permit by Friday is a long shot.' → Getting the import permit by Friday is ___.
